lede: Validation error levels off after latent size 32, and the scored model uses 128.
title: Autoencoder compression
question: How does latent size change reconstruction error on MNIST digits?
process: The autoencoder maps each image to one code and back again. The encoder compresses the 784 pixels, and the decoder turns that code back into an image:
Training minimizes the mean squared error between each image and its reconstruction:
There is no distribution over the code, and no KL term. The compression ratio is 784 divided by the length of the code.

On the saved validation curve, the error falls from about 0.187 at latent size 2 to 0.096 at latent size 128. The scored checkpoint uses latent size 128: test MSE 0.0414 and MAE 0.0771. The hyperparameter search recorded no finished trial.

opening.summary: Latent size 128 is marked. It has the lowest validation MSE on the saved curve, and it is the checkpoint that was scored. The hyperparameter search itself never finished a trial.
opening.hover: Latent size 128 is the marked point.

marks.answers: What didn't turn out as expected?
marks.summary: Latent size 2 is a 392× compression, and the validation MSE is 0.1867. A code that short keeps a blurry class average: the digit class may survive, but the stroke does not.

marks.answers: Why do you think the results might not be great?
marks.summary: Latent size 4 is a 196× compression, and the validation MSE is 0.1496. The bottleneck is still too small for stroke thickness and slant, so the error stays high.

marks.answers: How could the results be improved?
marks.summary: Latent size 8 is a 98× compression, and the validation MSE is 0.1154. This is the steep part of the curve. The next doublings are where digits usually become recognizable.
Latent size 16 is a 49× compression, and the validation MSE is 0.1042. This is where the useful range starts: a code of this length can hold thickness and slant.
Latent size 32 is a 24.5× compression, and the validation MSE is 0.0999. Digits are usually recognizable around 16 to 32. Past this point the curve is almost flat.

marks.answers: Why do you think the results might not be great?
marks.summary: Latent size 64 is a 12.25× compression, and the validation MSE is 0.0975. The drop from latent size 32 is only 0.0024. The extra coordinates are copying detail the decoder already approximated.

Latent size 128 is marked because it is the minimum of this validation curve, at MSE 0.0964, and it is the checkpoint that was evaluated. The compression is 6.12×. Test MSE is 0.0414 and test MAE is 0.0771. The drop from latent size 32 (0.0999) to here is 0.0035, so a practical code is already in the range 16 to 32. On the reconstruction grid for this checkpoint, 7, 2, 1, 0, 4, and 9 stay readable, and a little soft.
marks.hover: Latent size 128, 6.12× compression, validation MSE 0.0964, test MSE 0.0414.

reflection.worked: The training loss falls, and the latent-128 checkpoint copies a test digit at MSE 0.0414.
reflection.unexpected: Validation MSE only moves from 0.0975 at latent size 64 to 0.0964 at 128. The hyperparameter search has no finished trial, so hidden size, dropout, and learning rate were never scored.
reflection.why: Almost all of the drop on the saved curve is finished by latent size 16. The curve and the test score of 0.0414 come from different stages. A reasonable reading is that a digit stroke fits in about that many coordinates, so further ones have little left to store.
reflection.improve: For compression, stop near latent size 16 or 32. Finish the hyperparameter search before treating any other setting as tested. A sharper copy needs a different loss, not a longer code.
